content: Keloids are an overgrowth of scar tissue that develops at the site of a healed skin injury. They appear as raised, thickened areas of skin that can vary in color, including flesh-colored, red, or pink. These lesions typically form directly over the site of a previous wound or injury and may have a lumpy or ridged texture. During their formation and growth, keloids can cause itching. Keloids can result from various types of skin injuries, including acne, burns, chickenpox, ear piercings, minor scratches, surgical incisions, traumatic wounds, or even vaccination sites. Certain groups of people are at a higher risk of developing keloids. They are more commonly seen in individuals aged 10 to 20 years and are more prevalent among African Americans, Asians, and Hispanics. Additionally, there is often a familial tendency for keloids, meaning they can run in families. The term keloidosis is used when multiple or recurrent keloids occur. The diagnosis of keloids is typically made based on the appearance of the skin or scar. In some cases, a skin biopsy may be performed to rule out other types of skin growths, such as tumors. It is important to contact a healthcare provider if you develop keloids and are considering treatment to remove or reduce them, or if you experience new symptoms associated with the keloid. Treatment for keloids is not always necessary, as they are generally not harmful. However, if treatment is desired, several options are available to reduce their size or appearance. These include corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy (freezing), laser treatments, radiation therapy, or surgical removal. Keloids are not typically dangerous to health, but they can have cosmetic implications and may affect a person’s appearance. Over time, some keloids may become smaller, flatter, and less noticeable, though this process can take several years. Additionally, surgical removal of a keloid does not guarantee that it will not return, and in some cases, the resulting scar may be larger than the original keloid. Potential complications of keloids include changes in appearance, discomfort or tenderness, irritation caused by friction with clothing, limited mobility if the keloids are extensive, psychological distress due to their size or disfigurement, and the possibility of recurrence after treatment. Additionally, the use of imiquimod cream has shown promise in preventing keloids from forming after surgery or in preventing their recurrence following surgical removal.
